<reason>Both sides were competent, but CON (B) built and sustained the cleaner decisive structure. Its case rested on an absolute-defeating dilemma: either "never suspend" forbids the parked claim too (so a thin-staffed agency must pay a flagged, possibly hijacked, unrecoverable payment), or it permits withholding pending review, in which case the rule bans only the version that self-corrects on a deadline. PRO chose the first horn explicitly in A4.1 and repeated it in closing, and CON converted that concession into the most memorable weighing frame of the debate ("judge by what the flagged person actually lives through"; a clock versus a signature). CON also blunted PRO's strongest harm story by conceding carve-outs for medical and small recurring payments plus instant self-verification, which left PRO's rent-and-medication imagery mostly applying to cases CON no longer defends holding. On the automation-bias line, CON's charge that PRO's "meaningful review" is definitionally immune to failure, and that a recorded case-specific rationale is a form field that bias fills in confidently, went largely unanswered: PRO declined to supply any ex-ante auditable test (caseload cap, override rate) after being asked directly. PRO's best work was the principled reframe — screening versus deprivation, assessed individualized grounds versus suspicion alone, and the fair-comparison point that CON contrasts its ideal design with an already rule-violating rubber stamp. Those kept PRO alive and forced CON to answer the "certainty substituted for suspicion" charge. But PRO offered no concrete grounding examples at all, never defended why a bright-line "never" beats bounded, deadline-limited holds despite CON's counterexample logic, and its closing crystallized the very horn CON wanted. Format compliance was clean on both sides.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>CON's parked-claim dilemma (B2.3-B2.4, sharpened in B4.1-B4.2 and B5.1): PRO's answer that withholding pending review is itself a prohibited unreviewed suspension forced PRO to accept that on thin-staffing nights the flagged payment must go out, which CON turned into "never" mandating unrecoverable loss — a horn PRO never escaped, only re-described as CON assuming certainty.</best_rebuttal>
